title: Mailgun Pricing 2026: Free Plan, Tiers and Costs
summary: Mailgun pricing combines monthly fees with per-thousand overage charges. Compare all tier options and determine your total cost.
body_markdown:
## Mailgun upgrade volume threshold


Once the overage you would pay on your current plan, month after month, exceeds the extra price of stepping up, **the next Mailgun plan becomes cheaper** .


**Doing nothing has a cost** . If you stay on a plan after outgrowing its included volume, every extra email is billed at the overage rate.


Against that, the step-up price is a flat cost. So the break-even is simple: divide the price difference between the two plans by the overage rate per email, then add the result to the volume your current plan already includes.


For two moves, Basic to Foundation and Foundation to Scale, the chart shows that send count.


Read it as a tripwire. If your monthly sending sits below a bar, the lower plan is still cheaper even with overage. If you sit above it, you're paying a penalty for not upgrading.


Check your own sending against both bars, using a typical month rather than your best one. Look at the current rate card before you commit.


If you want that check automated and the connector for it doesn't exist, you needn't wait on a vendor's roadmap: Activepieces can build the missing integration with AI-generated code that stays private to your own instance, and its 747 integrations, counted from the open source monorepo, are roughly 60% community-contributed.


### When to stay put despite overage


If you cross your included volume only in a launch month or a seasonal rush, you pay the overage for a few weeks, while a higher plan charges its full price every month of the year.


**Overage isn't always a reason to upgrade** . Staying put is the cheaper call when the spikes are short and the quiet months are well under the limit.


It also makes sense to stay if the bigger plan's extras do nothing for you. Higher tiers come with more retention, more domains and other features, and paying for those only pays off if you'll use them.
